summary.text: A megatsunami is an extremely large wave made when a great mass of material suddenly falls into a body of water or right beside it.
Ordinary tsunamis come from earthquakes moving the sea floor and typically stay under about 30 m, while megatsunamis can start hundreds of metres high because the water is splashed up and out.
Landslides, meteor impacts and volcanic eruptions cause them, and in a confined bay or reservoir the water may be unable to spread out, producing exceedingly large waves.

facts.label: Common threshold
facts.value: Usually taken as waves over 100 metres high

facts.label: Prehistoric impacts
facts.value: May have made waves over 1,500 metres

facts.label: Definition
facts.value: Coined by media, with no precise definition

items.prompt: A rock slope collapses into a narrow mountain bay. Why can the wave be far taller than one from a big offshore earthquake?

options.label: Earthquakes only move water sideways, never upward
The falling mass splashes water up and the bay keeps it from spreading
The bay's tides add hundreds of metres to any wave
Rock heats the water so it swells upward quickly

items.explain: The sudden displacement splashes water upward and outward, and a confined body of water cannot let it disperse.

items.prompt: An undersea earthquake rarely causes a megatsunami, but a landslide it triggers next to the water can. Why?

options.label: Earthquakes happen too deep to reach the surface
Landslides only occur in shallow lakes
Earthquakes cancel out the waves they start
The landslide displaces a much larger amount of water

items.explain: Landslides beside water caused by quakes or eruptions displace far more water than the quake or eruption itself.

items.prompt: An ordinary tsunami passes under a ship in the deep open ocean. What does the crew most likely notice?

options.label: Possibly nothing, just a slight swell
A wall of water tens of metres high
The ship being pulled down into a trough
A loud roar followed by breaking surf

items.explain: Offshore, ordinary tsunamis form only a slight swell, so one could pass beneath a ship unnoticed.

items.prompt: How high did the water surge up the shore in the 1958 Lituya Bay megatsunami, the tallest ever recorded?

options.label: About 30 metres
About 52 metres
About 520 metres
About 5,200 metres

items.explain: It reached a run-up height of 520 metres, far above the roughly 30 m that ordinary tsunamis typically reach.

items.prompt: A landslide tsunami hits one stretch of coast with 15 m waves, yet farther away it is not a major hazard. Why does it fade so fast?

options.label: Landslide waves travel too slowly to go far
The landslide pulls the water back toward itself
Ocean currents always push such waves back
Its small source makes shorter waves that weaken with distance

items.explain: Most landslide tsunamis have a small source area, giving shorter wavelengths that radial damping reduces far away.

items.prompt: A wave is reported as 20 m high at sea but surging 80 m up a hillside. Which figure is the run-up height?

options.label: The 20 m height out at sea
The 80 m height reached on land
The 60 m difference between them
The 100 m total of the two

items.explain: Run-up height is how high the water surges when it meets land, which can be several times the wave's height near shore.
